explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron is firing on “document‐header” metadata lines – those all-caps or title-style snippets that label or flag a text as a blog, a court opinion (publish/unpublish notices, docket headings, court names), a bug-tracker helper note, a company “house” line, paper titles, etc. In short, it spots the formatted header or publication/status banner that sits atop many different document types.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron is essentially a “sentence‐start” detector: it lights up on the very first (capitalized) token at the beginning of a sentence or section.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on article‐metadata markers—stand-alone section labels and media bylines (e.g. “Image copyright AFP,” “Photo by…,” “Video,” “Opinion,” “Featured Reviews,” ad-solicitation headers, etc.) that signal captions or section headings rather than running text.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature fires on the very first article (e.g. “The,” occasionally “Any”) of formal section or document openings—typical “The X…” or “The present invention…” template intros in patents, abstracts and headlines—marking the start of a new document/section.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature isn’t about any single topic or domain word, but about “break‐points” in the text—i.e. the spots where one unit ends and another begins.  It lights up on prepositions or function words that introduce PPs (of, de, within), on the very first subword of longer content‐words (exc- in “excision,” emic in “anemic,” prob in “probability,” calculat- in “calculated,” etc.), on punctuation that delimits phrases (hyphens, quotes), and even on script or domain‐shift tokens (www, Cyrillic letters, Assyrian).  In effect it is a general boundary/segmentation detector marking the edges of morphemes, words, phrases or language‐style shifts.

explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on tokens that begin new sentences or segments—i.e. the first (usually capitalized) word or opening quote of a sentence.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron detects the very first token of a new content block—e.g. the opening word or symbol of a headline, section heading, code comment or block quote—marking “start-of-line” or “segment-beginning.”
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron is a “heading-end” detector: it lights up on the key label word at the end of section titles or headings (e.g. “Description” in “Product Description,” “Plastics” in “Facial Plastics,” “Invention” in patent headings, named‐entity titles, code-comment titles, Q&A subject lines, etc.).

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires whenever you’re at the very start of a sentence or heading on a capitalized word—often on the first subword of a proper noun or other word whose initial letter is uppercase.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature appears to fire on those small, high‐frequency subword tokens that serve as affixes or stand-alone function words across many contexts—things like the “-son” in Davidson, “-mer” in Khmer, “ney” in McKinney, the French/Spanish prepositions “de/du,” the ampersand joiner “&,” URL‐parameter markers like “doi,” and code verbs like “copy” or “count.”  In effect it is a kind of boundary/morpheme detector that lights up on short BPE pieces that often mark the ends of stems or act as atomic function words.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature detects the first word of a section heading or title—i.e. it lights up on the initial token of headlines or bolded section headers.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature picks out subword pieces that mark the start of “named” or “definitional” units—whether in prose (personal‐name fragments like “Di,” “Van,” “Claude,” accented pieces like “ö/ä/ç/ı”) or in code (the Python/LaTeX keyword “def,” Java’s “Def” in error names, the “@” scope in JS imports). In effect it signals the boundary where a new entity or definition is being introduced.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron is a “suffix detector” for multi‐subtoken content words. It strongly activates on the second (usually final) BPE piece of longer English words—-ical, ‑ine, ‑ize, ‑ers, ‑ery, etc.—which tend to carry the key grammatical or semantic signal (professions, scientific terms, titles, headlines) in formal and technical text.
explanations.negative_explanation: This head is essentially a “line-start” detector: it lights up on tokens that begin a new block or section—whether a Wikipedia article title (“Lo”), a code import or directive (“from”, “@”), an HTML tag (“<”), or a capitalized heading/name (“V…”, “Jay”, “O…”, “Kal…”).

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on tokens that serve as explicit section or heading labels—e.g. patent section titles (“Field of the Invention,” “Descriptions of the Related Art”), case-citation metadata lines (“Decided,” “Appeals”), roman-numeral list markers (“i)”, “ii)”) or dictionary headwords—i.e. structural title markers that introduce a new document section.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature detects line-initial structural markers that kick off new sections or blocks—e.g. CSS/SCSS at-rules like “@import”, headings/titles (Legend:, Next.js, Stars…, Vuxenutbildning:), big comment-box delimiters (“/*****…”), section or example labels (“Suppose…”), etc. It fires on tokens that serve as block-boundary or section-header cues.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on square-bracketed scientific/medical paper titles—e.g. “[Primary gastrointestinal lymphoma]” or “[Subarachnoid hemorrhage …]”—i.e. the pattern of a research-article title in brackets, often with capitalized technical terms and hyphenated compounds.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron strongly fires on lexical items naming or addressing human agents—especially collective or role‐based nouns (workers, employees, people) and the personal pronouns “you,” “we,” etc. In other words, it flags references to people as actors or addressees.

explanations.positive_explanation:
Here’s a concise abstract for each high-activation token feature:

• Feature “But” (1.000): marks a sentence‐initial contrastive conjunction, signaling a pivot or objection in discourse.  
• Feature “And” (0.996): flags a sentence‐initial additive conjunction, used to continue or append information.  
• Feature “that” (0.987): signals a clausal connector (demonstrative or subordinating), introducing explanations, relative clauses, or reported content.  
• Feature “Whether” (0.985): identifies a sentence‐initial subordinating conjunction that introduces alternatives or conditional clauses.  
• Feature “Why” (0.984): marks an interrogative/explanatory clause opener, signaling a request for reason or cause.  
• Feature “With” (0.984): flags a sentence‐initial prepositional phrase that sets context by specifying accompaniment, means, or conditions.  
• Feature “and” (0.983): detects a lowercase coordinating conjunction linking items or sub-problems in enumerated/math-question lists.  
• Feature “H” (0.980): fires on an uppercase “H” at the start of headings or proper nouns beginning with H (place names, titles, section markers).  
• Feature “i” (0.979): highlights a lowercase “i” used either as the first‐person pronoun or as a product/brand‐name prefix.  
• Feature “Russia” (0.979): identifies the proper noun “Russia,” i.e. a geopolitical entity.  
• Feature “T” (0.978): detects an uppercase “T” at the start of a proper name or title beginning with T (e.g. band names).
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron is simply flagging “continuation” BPE subtokens – the little 2–4-letter fragments you see inside words (hem in “ischemic,” “Nohemi,” “Chrysanthemum,” “Mayhem,” schema/​schem–as, etc.; leg in “Allegro,” ever in “beverage,” lam in “Neflamapimod,” isk in “risk,” ru in “Druid,” reverse, etc.). In other words, it detects that the current token is not a standalone word but a word-internal subword piece.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron is essentially a “block‐start” detector: it spikes on the very first word of a new text chunk (often a headline or paragraph opening), regardless of whether it’s capitalized or not.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on typographic emphasis/formatting markers—e.g. bolded or asterisk‐delimited words, separator lines, option labels etc.—i.e. on tokens visually highlighted via asterisks or similar markup.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on sentence-initial “hook” words—single-token discourse markers (e.g. Want, While, With, In) that introduce questions, contrasts or context as opening connectors.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires whenever the model sees the “**” double‐asterisk marker used in plain-text markup (Markdown/Wiki style) to denote emphasis, boldface, footnote ends, section breaks, etc.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron is a classic “subword‐continuation” detector: it fires on BPE pieces that continue a larger word (especially common suffixes like ­ions, ­ving, ­amine, ­ires, ­itors, etc.) and is suppressed on the first piece of a word.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on tokens that begin a new segment—whether a section or article title, a list entry, a code import line, or the first word of a question—i.e. it flags the very first token of a heading/paragraph/statement.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron specializes in spotting title- or heading-style tokens—those high-level labels and metadata bits (headlines, section titles, captions, dates, copyright notices, etc.) that structure a document rather than its running prose.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron is a detector for the “de la” pattern—i.e. the feminine singular definite article “la” immediately following the preposition “de” (the “of the” construction in Spanish/French).

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires whenever the text is introducing or “declaring” a new named entity—whether it’s the title of a Wikipedia entry, a product heading, a news‐headline tag, an import or class/function signature in code, etc.  In every case you see a bolded or otherwise marked name immediately followed by parentheses (for pronunciation, type parameters or function arguments), signalling “here comes the definition or declaration” of that entity.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature is firing on parenthetical metadata—i.e. the bits of text you stick in “(…)” or “[…]” to supply acronyms, citations, version or license tags, attributions, etc., in formal/legal/academic prose.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron simply spots tokens whose first character is a capital “S” (e.g. “Sonic,” “Skeletal,” “Surgical,” “Skegness,” etc.).
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron responds to subword affixes—common prefixes (pro-, pre-, inter-, etc.) and suffixes (-at(ion), ‑wards, ‑how, ‑den, ‑ner, SQL keywords like SELECT, etc.)—i.e. it flags morphemic building blocks rather than full lexical roots.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature detects tokens that open a new block—e.g. the very first word of a paragraph, section heading, license header or standalone line—marking “start-of-block” boundaries in the text.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature detects the opening volume number of a formal court‐reporter citation—i.e. the leading numeric token in strings like “645 So.2d 940 (1994),” “164 F.3d 719 (2011),” “377 Md 293 (2012),” etc.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature detects tokens that kick off a new structural block or directive at the start of a line—e.g. line-leading markers for scripts and markup (<?xml, <script>, <!DOCTYPE>, comments), batch directives (@Echo, Set), imports/requires, and section-heading words (Search, Legend, Inside, etc.).
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature detects sentence-initial connective or pivot words (often adverbs or interjections like “Well,” “However,” “Yesterday,” “Leaving,” “And,” etc.) that signal a rhetorical transition or new discourse segment.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron is a “formatting-and-shorthand” detector: it lights up on runs of non-alphanumeric border or decoration characters (pipes, dashes, underscores, equals, stars, etc.) used in ASCII-art, comment blocks or tables, and on short domain-specific subwords or acronyms (e.g. the Arabic name particle “bin,” function/space names like “Sym,” enzyme subunits “M,” tool names like “FOAM,” “istar” in Wistar, etc.). It flags structural or highly specialized tokens rather than ordinary prose.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature is a line‐start detector: it turns on for any token that begins a new line (whether it’s “/” in code paths, “import” in Python/JS, uppercase headings or place names, markdown “##”/“===” markers, legal‐citation numbers, news‐article datelines, etc.).

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on the single‐character uppercase subword token when it appears at the start of a word or label (e.g. the “R” in Rural/Rafted/Rational or the “Q” in “Q:”), effectively marking the leading letter of capitalized headings, titles or question tags.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature detects uppercase initialisms and acronyms—especially paired forms joined by “&” (e.g. J & K, S & P, Q & A, AT & T)—i.e. named‐entity labels built from capital letters.
